newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dlr/yen seen well-supported in Asia.
newsitem.headline: Dlr/yen seen well-supported in Asia.

text.p: The dollar is expected to maintain a firm tone in Asia on Friday, but activity may be slow ahead of a long weekend in Japan, traders said.
Japanese financial markets will be closed on Monday for a national holiday.
Dollar/yen is likely to be capped by Japanese exporter offers which are expected to emerge above 116.40 yen, but bargain-hunting interest could limit the downside at around 115.50 yen, traders said.
Japanese institutional investors are still keen to buy dollars on dips to unwind their hedges, traders said.

"On Thursday, some players had hoped to buy dollars on dips after the trade data, but those hopes were dashed as the dollar rose sharply in reaction to a smaller-than-expected surplus," said a trader at a long-term bank.

Japan's trade surplus in June rose 27.7 percent year-on-year to 934.21 billion yen, the Finance Ministry said on Thursday. Economists' forecasts had ranged from 971.0 billion yen to 1.61 trillion yen.
In New York on Thursday, the dollar closed at 115.85/95 yen, after trading above the 116 yen threshold for much of the day.
U.S. trade data for May will be released at 1230 GMT Friday, but Tokyo operators expect the data to have limited impact on the forex market.
"Tonight's data is for May. We have already seen the June figure for Japan yesterday. People are becoming less concerned about the U.S.-Japan trade imbalance," said a trader at a trust bank.
Traders expect the dollar to trade in a relatively narrow range against the mark in Asia due a lack of fresh incentives.
"Pre-weekend profit-taking could push the dollar below 1.79 marks," the trust bank trader said.
In New York trade on Thursday, the dollar edged modestly lower in a range-bound session, failing repeatedly to push back above the 1.80 mark level.
Remarks from Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer and talk that European central banks were propping up the German currency also weighed on dollar/mark overnight.

Tietmeyer said on Thursday that he hoped the current upward "correction" of the dollar against the mark would not go too far and warned that officials were watching developments in the foreign exchange market closely.
